blocks.text: The last lesson, Feature Creation, was all about making more columns out of what you already had, a profit margin here, an age bucket there, an interaction feature somewhere else. This lesson is its direct counterpart, and it does almost the opposite job. Instead of asking what new column could you build, it asks a harder question: out of everything sitting in your dataframe right now, including the columns you just engineered, which ones actually deserve a seat at the table when you train a model. Feature creation grows your feature set. Feature selection shrinks it back down, on purpose, to only what earns its place.

blocks.alt: Raw columns branching into feature creation which adds more columns and feature selection which keeps fewer columns
blocks.caption: Two lessons, two directions. One grows your feature set, the other trims it down to what matters.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Feature selection is the practice of deliberately choosing a subset of the columns available to you, and leaving the rest out of training entirely. It sounds almost like a step backward after spending a whole lesson learning to create new columns, but the two skills work together. Once you have engineered every feature you can reasonably justify, you almost always end up with more columns than you started with, and not every one of them is going to help. Some will be dead weight. Some will just repeat information another column already carries. Feature selection is how you find those columns and cut them loose before a model ever sees them.
1.1 More Features Is Not Automatically Better

It is tempting to assume that handing a model more information can only help. More columns, more context, more chances to find a pattern, right. In practice that intuition breaks down fast, and the reason has a name: the curse of dimensionality. As you add more and more feature columns, the space a model has to search through to find a good pattern grows enormously, and the amount of data you actually have to fill that space does not grow anywhere near as fast. A model faced with hundreds of thin, mostly irrelevant columns has a much harder time separating real signal from pure coincidence than a model looking at a dozen genuinely useful ones.

More irrelevant or redundant features can genuinely hurt a model's ability to generalize to new data it has not seen before. They add noise the model has to wade through on every prediction. They slow down training significantly, since every extra column is extra computation on every single row, every single pass. And they make a model meaningfully harder to interpret, because now you have to explain a decision in terms of fifty inputs instead of eight. More is not free. Every column you keep has to earn that cost back.

blocks.alt: Too many irrelevant features leading to added noise, slower training, harder interpretation, and worse generalization
blocks.caption: The curse of dimensionality in one picture. Extra columns are never neutral, they always cost something.

blocks.title: More is not free
blocks.content: It is easy to think of unused columns as harmless, just sitting there doing nothing. They are not neutral. Every column you feed a model adds noise it has to filter through, computation it has to pay for, and complexity you have to explain later. Cutting a genuinely useless column is a pure win, not a tradeoff.

blocks.text: 1.2 What This Lesson Covers

This lesson works through four practical techniques for trimming a feature set down, roughly in order from simplest to most systematic, all of them implementable with pandas and NumPy alone, plus one standard scikit-learn tool worth knowing about.

items: Removing zero and near zero variance columns, the simplest possible filter
Removing highly correlated redundant features using a correlation matrix between features
Checking correlation between each feature and the target column as a relevance filter
Variance thresholding as a more formal, systematic version of the near zero variance idea

blocks.text: It closes with a worked example on a realistic, feature rich dataset that runs all three pandas techniques back to back and ends with a visibly smaller, more focused set of columns than it started with.
2. Removing Zero and Near Zero Variance Columns

Start with the easiest case there is. A column where almost every single row holds the exact same value carries essentially no information for a model to learn from. If a signup_country column reads USD for every row in your dataset, a model cannot possibly use it to distinguish one row from another, because there is nothing to distinguish. Every row looks identical on that one column. This is called zero variance, or near zero variance when a handful of rows differ but the overwhelming majority still sit on one repeated value.

blocks.alt: A column where almost every row holds the exact same repeated value flowing into near zero variance and essentially no signal
blocks.caption: A column that barely changes cannot help a model tell rows apart. It is dead weight, and it is the easiest kind to spot.

blocks.text: 2.1 Spotting Dead Columns With .var and .nunique

Pandas gives you two extremely quick ways to flag these columns. .var() computes the statistical variance of a numeric column, and a variance at or near zero means the values barely move at all. .nunique() counts how many distinct values a column holds, numeric or not, and a column where nunique() returns 1 is holding exactly one repeated value across every row, no exceptions.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'user_id': [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
    'signup_country': ['US', 'US', 'US', 'US', 'US'],
    'age': [25, 34, 45, 29, 51],
    'is_active': [1, 1, 1, 1, 1],
})

print(df.var(numeric_only=True))
print(df.nunique())

blocks.text: The output tells the story immediately. is_active has a variance of exactly 0.0, since every row holds the same value, 1. signup_country is not numeric so it does not show up in .var() at all, but .nunique() reports 1 for it, the same dead giveaway in a different tool. age, by contrast, has real spread in both its variance and its unique value count, meaning it is genuinely carrying information from row to row.
2.2 Dropping the Dead Weight

Once you have flagged the offenders, dropping them is a one line operation. Use .var() for your numeric columns and .nunique() for everything else, since a constant text column will never show up in a numeric variance check at all.

code.content:
near_zero_var_cols = df.var(numeric_only=True)
dead_numeric_cols = near_zero_var_cols[near_zero_var_cols < 0.01].index.tolist()

single_value_cols = [c for c in df.columns if df[c].nunique() <= 1]

df = df.drop(columns=list(set(dead_numeric_cols + single_value_cols)))
print(df.columns.tolist())

blocks.title: Numeric variance and nunique are not interchangeable
blocks.content: A variance threshold only makes sense on numeric columns, and it will silently skip anything that is not numeric unless you pass numeric_only correctly. .nunique() works on every column type, numeric or text, but it only catches the extreme case of a single repeated value, not a column that is merely close to constant with a wide numeric spread hiding one dominant value. Use both, and eyeball value_counts() on anything borderline before you commit to dropping it.

blocks.text: 3. Removing Highly Correlated Redundant Features

The next filter builds directly on correlation, something you already have some working knowledge of from earlier in this course. If two feature columns are extremely highly correlated with each other, close to 1 or close to negative 1, they are largely carrying the same information twice. Keeping both adds redundancy to your feature set without adding any real new signal for the model to work with. This lesson only goes deep enough into correlation to use it as a practical filter. The dedicated Correlation Analysis lesson coming up next in this module covers correlation itself in real depth.

blocks.alt: Feature X and feature Y both feeding into a correlation matrix that reveals a correlation near one and flags a redundant pair
blocks.caption: A correlation matrix is how you catch two columns that are quietly saying the same thing twice.

blocks.text: 3.1 Building a Correlation Matrix With df.corr

df.corr() computes the pairwise correlation between every numeric column in a dataframe, all at once, and returns the result as a square matrix. Every row and column pairing shows how strongly those two columns move together.

The matrix comes back showing square_footage and square_meters correlated at essentially 1.0. That is not a coincidence, it is a unit conversion of the exact same underlying measurement. A model that gets both columns is not getting two different pieces of information about a home, it is getting the same piece of information twice, once in feet and once in meters.
3.2 Deciding Which of a Redundant Pair to Drop

Once a correlation matrix flags a redundant pair, the fix is simple: keep one of the two and drop the other. Which one you keep is mostly a judgment call, favor whichever is more directly interpretable to whoever reads the model later, or whichever is cheaper and more reliable to collect at prediction time. Here, keeping square_footage and dropping square_meters is a reasonable default, since square footage is the more common unit in this dataset's market.

blocks.alt: Feature X and a highly correlated feature Y both feeding into a model input that gains no new signal from keeping both
blocks.caption: Two columns saying the same thing does not double the signal a model gets. It just doubles the redundancy.

blocks.title: Correlation analysis gets its own lesson right after this one
blocks.content: A single correlation number close to 1 is a strong, practical signal to act on, but it is a simplified read. Real correlation matrices on real datasets can have several near-redundant pairs at once, and choosing which member of each pair to keep can get more nuanced than a single rule of thumb. The Correlation Analysis lesson right after this one covers that in the depth it deserves. For now, treat anything above roughly 0.9 or below roughly negative 0.9 between two features as worth a second look.

blocks.text: 4. Feature Versus Target Correlation as a Relevance Filter

So far both filters looked only at the feature columns among themselves. This one brings the actual target column into the picture, the thing you are trying to predict. Computing a correlation matrix specifically between each feature and the target gives you a simple, genuinely useful relevance filter. A feature with a correlation close to zero against the target is a weak candidate on its own, since it barely moves in step with the very thing you are trying to model.

blocks.alt: A feature and a target column both feeding into a correlation with target check that produces a near zero score and a weak candidate flag
blocks.caption: If a feature barely moves with the target, it has little to offer a model on its own.

blocks.text: 4.1 Computing Feature to Target Correlation
The mechanics are almost identical to the feature versus feature check from the previous section, just read one specific row or column of the result back out, the one matching your target.

tenure_months and monthly_charges both come back with a real, sizeable correlation against churn, which lines up with the intuition that shorter tenure and higher monthly charges genuinely relate to whether someone cancels. favorite_color_code comes back with a correlation near zero, which is exactly what you would expect from a column that has nothing meaningful to do with the outcome. It is a solid candidate to drop.
4.2 The Linear Relationship Limitation

Here is the real limitation you have to keep in mind before you drop anything based on this filter alone. Correlation only captures linear relationships. It measures how closely a straight line describes the relationship between a feature and the target. A feature can be genuinely powerful in a nonlinear way, moving the target strongly in a curve, a threshold, or some other non straight-line pattern, while still showing a low simple correlation score, because a straight line is just the wrong shape to describe what that feature is actually doing.

blocks.alt: A nonlinear feature scoring a low linear correlation and looking like a weak feature while actually holding a genuinely predictive pattern
blocks.caption: Correlation only sees straight lines. A feature can be quietly powerful in a curve and still score close to zero.

blocks.title: Correlation only captures linear relationships
blocks.content: This is the single most important caveat in this entire lesson. A near zero correlation with the target is a helpful first filter, not a final verdict. Do not treat it as proof a feature is useless. Treat it as a flag worth a second look, ideally alongside a nonlinear model's own feature importance output, before you commit to dropping anything on correlation alone.

blocks.text: 5. Variance Thresholding as a Formal Tool

Section 2 dropped dead columns by hand, computing variance and nunique yourself and deciding on a cutoff as you went. Variance thresholding is a slightly more formal, systematic version of that exact same idea, and it is worth knowing the standard tool for doing it at scale once your dataset grows past a handful of columns you can eyeball.

blocks.alt: Many columns feeding into a VarianceThreshold step that applies a formal cutoff and drops low variance columns
blocks.caption: Same idea as computing variance by hand, just packaged into one reusable, systematic step.

blocks.text: 5.1 scikit-learn's VarianceThreshold

VarianceThreshold, from sklearn.feature_selection, is the standard tool for this at scale. You give it a threshold, fit it on your numeric feature columns, and it hands back a boolean mask telling you exactly which columns cleared the bar and which did not.

code.content:
from sklearn.feature_selection import VarianceThreshold

numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include='number').columns

selector = VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01)
selector.fit(df[numeric_cols])

kept_columns = numeric_cols[selector.get_support()]
print(kept_columns.tolist())

blocks.text: For a small, hand-inspectable dataset, computing .var() yourself and eyeballing the result is often faster and perfectly fine. VarianceThreshold starts earning its keep once you have dozens or hundreds of numeric columns and need one reusable, repeatable step you can drop straight into a preprocessing pipeline rather than a one-off manual check.
6. Worked Example: Narrowing Down a Feature Rich Dataset

Time to put all three pandas techniques from this lesson to work together, back to back, on one dataset. A real estate dataset arrives with a price target and six feature columns. Some of those columns are dead weight, one pair is quietly redundant, and one is barely related to price at all. None of that is obvious just from glancing at the raw dataframe. It only becomes obvious once you actually run the checks.

blocks.alt: A feature rich dataset passing through a variance filter, a correlation filter, and a target relevance filter to reach a focused feature set
blocks.caption: Three filters, applied in sequence, on the exact same dataset. Each one earns its place before the next runs.

blocks.text: 6.1 The Raw Data

Six feature columns sit alongside price, the target: square_footage, square_meters, bedrooms, bathrooms, year_built, listing_currency, and lucky_number. That is seven columns total once you count price itself. Not every one of those six features deserves to reach a model.
6.2 Dropping Zero and Near Zero Variance Columns
Run the same check from section 2 across the whole dataset. listing_currency reads USD in every single row, so it should jump out immediately.

code.content:
single_value_cols = [c for c in data.columns if data[c].nunique() <= 1]
print(single_value_cols)   # ['listing_currency']

data = data.drop(columns=single_value_cols)
print(data.columns.tolist())

blocks.text: listing_currency is gone. It never carried any information a model could use in the first place, since every home in this dataset is listed in the exact same currency.
6.3 Dropping a Redundant Correlated Pair
Next, build a correlation matrix across the remaining numeric feature columns and look for anything sitting close to 1 or negative 1.
square_footage and square_meters come back correlated at 1.0, exactly as expected, since one is a straight unit conversion of the other. Drop one of the two.
6.4 Checking Feature Versus Target Correlation
Finally, check each remaining feature against price itself, the target this whole dataset exists to predict.

square_footage, bedrooms, and bathrooms all come back strongly correlated with price, which matches real-world intuition about what drives a home's value. year_built shows a moderate correlation, real but weaker. lucky_number, unsurprisingly given its name, comes back correlated with price at barely above zero. It is flagged as a weak candidate and dropped.
6.5 Before and After
Line the two feature sets up side by side and the reduction is immediate. Six feature columns walked in. Four walked out, each one having earned its place through an actual check rather than a guess.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Stage","Feature Columns"],"rows":[["Before selection","square_footage, square_meters, bedrooms, bathrooms, year_built, lucky_number"],["After selection","square_footage, bedrooms, bathrooms, year_built"]]}

blocks.alt: Six feature columns before selection narrowing down through selection steps to four feature columns after selection
blocks.caption: Same dataset, same target, a third fewer columns, and every one still in the mix is pulling real weight.

blocks.text: Nothing about the model or the target changed. The only thing that changed is which columns get to compete for the model's attention, and that alone is often enough to produce a model that trains faster, generalizes better, and is genuinely easier to explain to somebody else.
7. Recap

blocks.alt: A variance filter, correlation between features, correlation with target, and VarianceThreshold at scale all feeding into a selected feature set
blocks.caption: Four ideas from this lesson, all aimed at the same goal, a feature set with nothing riding along for free.

items: Feature selection is the counterpart to feature creation, choosing intelligently which columns deserve to reach a model rather than adding more of them
More features is not automatically better, the curse of dimensionality means irrelevant or redundant columns add noise, slow training, and hurt generalization and interpretability
A column with zero or near zero variance carries essentially no information, and .var() or .nunique() catch these dead columns in seconds
A correlation matrix between features flags redundant pairs close to 1 or negative 1, where keeping both columns adds no real new signal
A correlation matrix between each feature and the target is a simple relevance filter, but it only captures linear relationships, so a low score is a first filter, not a final verdict
VarianceThreshold from scikit-learn is the standard, systematic tool for the same near zero variance idea once a dataset grows past what you can eyeball by hand
The worked example took a six-feature dataset down to four by running variance, feature correlation, and target correlation checks in sequence, each one removing exactly what it was designed to catch
